title: Channelrhodopsin-style optically gated access with waveguide wordlines
idea: Optogenetics opens ion channels with light; replace the electrically gated access device with a wide-gap a-SiC:H photoconductor (PECVD at 250 C) between bitline and storage node, lit row by row through SiN waveguide wordlines fed by an on-package laser and modulator.
why: In the dark the wide-gap film has almost no thermal generation and there is no gate at all, so GIDL and electrical wordline coupling vanish: off-current approaches 1e-20 A (refresh-free), the 3 V wordline CV2 is gone, and row hammer coupling disappears.

title: Convert DRAM capacitor-module tool bays into capacitorless 3D tiers
idea: Po: the fab throws away its capacitor tools. In an existing DRAM fab, retire the high-aspect-ratio capacitor etch, high-k and TiN modules and reuse the bays for stacked capacitorless floating-body tiers built from epitaxial Si/SiGe superlattices, leaving the periphery line unchanged.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: removes the 60-75:1 etch and ~15-20% of process steps and turns sunk fab space into 3D capacity years faster than a new fab.

title: Substitute hard-switched refresh with LC resonant charge recovery
idea: Substitute CV^2-dissipating drivers with adiabatic resonant drive: an inductor on the package or interposer resonates with wordline and bitline capacitance. Two subarrays refresh in antiphase, so energy swings back and forth between them instead of burning in drivers.
why: Refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and voltage floor: recovers ~50-70% of refresh-burst CV^2. Refresh is periodic and schedulable, which suits resonant drive.

title: Minify charged cells: discharge-biased coding skips empty-row refresh
idea: The controller encodes each line (XOR with a learned base plus bus-invert, polarity flipped for true/anti-cell subarrays) so >90% of cells sit in the discharged, non-leaking state, and a per-row flag marks rows with no charged cells, which are never refreshed.
why: Only charged cells need refresh; zero-heavy and sparse tensor data yields 2-5x fewer refreshed rows.

title: Innkeeper's rule: house the restless guests in the weak rows
idea: An innkeeper puts the up-all-night guests in the rooms by the noisy street. The controller profiles weak rows and remaps the hottest pages (touched more often than every 16 ms) into them, since every activation restores charge; strong rows hold cold data, and the global refresh period is set by strong rows only.
why: Turns natural activations into free refresh: the global interval can stretch 2-4x, with a fallback refresh only when a weak row goes quiet.

title: Colors pick the layer: wavelength-addressed 3D stacks without staircases
idea: Inverts 'each 3D tier needs its own wired wordline contact': give each tier a photoconductive access element made of quantum dots tuned to a distinct absorption band (16 tiers, 16 wavelengths) and run a light pipe per column, so choosing the wavelength selects the tier and all tiers share their electrical lines with no staircase or tier-specific masks.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier wiring (fact 2), allowing 16-64 tiers at single-tier mask count, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: optical crosstalk, us-class access, dot stability.

title: On-die microheaters anneal variable-retention-time defects in situ
idea: Borrow PCM-style TiN heaters under each subarray. After migrating the subarray's data, pulse it to 300-400 C for microseconds to milliseconds to re-passivate hydrogen-related traps behind the VRT and leakage tail.
why: VRT forces a 2-4x refresh guardband. Periodic healing shrinks the tail so the refresh interval can grow 2-4x over the part's life.

title: Back-gate dynamic threshold on existing 22/28 nm FD-SOI lines
idea: Rearrange threshold control from fixed doping to a live back gate: build 1T1C eDRAM cells with MIM capacitors on existing 22FDX/28FDS FD-SOI processes, holding the array's back-gate well at strong reverse bias in hold (Vt +250-300 mV) and switching it to forward bias only for the subarray being accessed. The thin BOX also isolates the storage node from the substrate, so there is no storage-node junction leakage.
why: Hold off-current falls ~100x while access speed is preserved (fact 3), using foundry capacity available today (Dresden, Crolles, Malta NY).

title: Antimony delta-doped tunnel diodes make a bistable, refresh-free storage node
idea: Sb: grow series pairs of Si/SiGe resonant interband tunnel diodes (Sb and B delta-doped layers) epitaxially on each storage node; their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages held by a ~pA sustain current, so the node self-restores, and every critical dimension is an epitaxial thickness.
why: Replaces periodic refresh (fact 3) with a static hold of ~4 mW/GB at 1 pA/cell; device dimensions come from epitaxy, so no EUV is needed (fact 4).

title: Minify the channel to one atomic layer: MoS2 vertical access
idea: Shrink the access-transistor body to a 0.65 nm MoS2/WSe2 monolayer wrapped gate-all-around on the pillar sidewall; with no bulk volume and no doped junctions, subthreshold and junction-generation leakage both collapse. Semimetal Bi/Sb contacts keep on-current above ~20 uA.
why: Leakage tail (<=13 fA) targeted below 0.1 fA; retention 64 ms -> ~10 s, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss by >90%.

title: Anodic alumina self-ordered pores template vertical gate-all-around access pillars
idea: Al: anodize a deposited aluminum film so it self-organizes into hexagonal nanopores (pitch 25-100 nm, set by anodizing voltage), guided by a coarse DUV pre-pattern, and use the pores as a mold or hard mask for vertical channel pillars wrapped by a gate.
why: Gives ~25-40 nm pitch vertical access arrays with no EUV (fact 4) at near-zero mask cost; hexagonal packing is ~15% denser than square, with domain-boundary defects handled by redundancy.

title: Compiler-tagged ephemeral memory that is never refreshed
idea: TRIZ #34 Discarding and recovering: let data that will die anyway go unrefreshed. Compilers and AI runtimes place allocations whose lifetime is shorter than guaranteed retention (activations, KV-cache blocks overwritten each step, staging buffers) in an 'ephemeral' region whose rows the controller never refreshes, with a hardware write-timestamp that faults reads of expired data.
why: Much of AI memory traffic is short-lived (Facts 3, 5): claim 30-70% fewer refreshes in accelerator memory and recovered bandwidth, with no device change.

title: Pheromone-evaporation allocator expires short-lived data without refresh
idea: Ant trails evaporate on purpose; an allocator API (malloc_ttl) places data with lifetime shorter than retention (activations, scratch KV, network buffers living 1-20 ms) in rows whose refresh is disabled by an 'evaporating' bit, and the row traps on read after its TTL.
why: On AI accelerators activation memory is 30-60% of the footprint; making it refresh-free cuts refresh energy ~40% and returns bandwidth.

title: Indium-free zinc-tin-oxide access transistors stacked as relaxed-pitch tiers
idea: Zn: use amorphous ZnSnO, made of abundant zinc and tin, as the access-transistor channel in BEOL tiers patterned by ArF immersion at F~20-30 nm; ZTO off-current ~1e-19 A/um gives seconds-to-minutes retention, so each tier uses a small planar capacitor and density comes from 8-16 tiers instead of EUV shrink.
why: Avoids indium/gallium and EUV chokepoints (fact 4, resources) and cuts refresh ~1000x (fact 3); going beyond IGZO gain cells by deleting scarce elements from the channel.

title: Acoustic charge transport conveyor for refresh, revived from delay lines
idea: Revive mercury and magnetostrictive delay-line memory, together with 1980s acoustic charge transport: a surface acoustic wave launched across a piezoelectric overlayer carries charge packets from storage wells down a column to one regenerating amplifier and back. Refresh becomes continuous recirculation through one amplifier per column instead of row activations.
why: Refresh energy concentrates in one optimized regenerator per column, and transport is driven by a single transducer (fact 3); targets 3-5x lower refresh energy, with refresh fully hidden from the command bus.

title: Onion-shell 3D access devices: one etch, one clean, many tiers
idea: Random stimulus 'onion': many layers around one core, peeled at once. In a vertical-bitline 3D DRAM the access transistors of all ~32 tiers are concentric gate-all-around shells around one bitline hole, defined by a single hole etch, one dry clean and one conformal channel/gate deposition, with each tier's wordline a lateral plane.
why: Wet steps per wafer are nearly tier-independent, so water per bit falls ~1/N: 32 tiers gives >10x less water per bit while attacking the missing manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2).

title: Retention-certified DRAM grades sold at a premium
idea: Use legacy test flows to bin dies by measured retention (256 ms, 1 s at 45 C) and program the refresh setting into SPD. Long-retention bins go to battery devices; leaky bins go to cooled data centers.
why: Monetizes the existing retention spread with zero capex, cutting refresh energy ~75% in the premium segment.

title: Magnify Vt shift to latch the access device permanently off
idea: Insert a thin HZO ferroelectric in each access-transistor gate stack; on power loss one global wordline pulse flips every access gate into a +1.2 V Vt-shifted deep-off state, trapping capacitor charge behind <1e-21 A leakage until power returns and a reset pulse restores normal Vt.
why: Turns conventional 1T1C into a power-loss-surviving memory with one FE switch per power cycle; also reduces refresh in operation.

title: Dendritic-spine-neck quantum-confined access channel
idea: Spine necks isolate synapses by being long and ultra-thin; make the access channel a 1.5-2 nm-thick Si ribbon segment where quantum confinement widens the effective bandgap from 1.12 eV toward ~1.6-2 eV, while wider source/drain 'heads' stay bulk-like for low resistance.
why: Intrinsic carrier density, band-to-band tunneling and GIDL fall exponentially with gap, lowering the off-current tail 100-1000x and giving retention of seconds; the cost is mobility and monolayer-thickness Vt variation.

title: Williams tube read-around fix: analog row-hammer integrators
idea: Williams tubes failed partly because reading one spot disturbed its neighbors (the 'read-around ratio'), so refresh had to be set by worst-case counts. Give each DRAM row driver a tiny leaky capacitor that receives a charge packet on every neighboring activation and decays over time. When its voltage crosses a comparator threshold, the driver requests a targeted refresh of that row.
why: Row-hammer protection (rows flip after ~1k ACTs) for 1T+1C+comparator per row instead of SRAM counter tables, and refresh goes only where disturbance has built up. Claimed <0.5% die area versus 2-5% for counter-based schemes.

title: AR-glasses budget: drop the negative-wordline pump and cut VPP
idea: AR glasses have milliwatt memory budgets. Lower the wordline high from ~3 V to ~2.2 V and remove the negative-wordline charge pump, lowering access Vt to keep write speed; the higher off-current and occasional incomplete writes push raw BER toward 1%, which the code tolerates.
why: Facts 7 and 10: pumps run at ~30-40% efficiency, so wordline energy falls ~45%, pump area shrinks a few % of the die, and gate-oxide and GIDL stress drop.

title: Temperature-adaptive ECC turns spare bits into stronger code when hot
idea: Worse at 125 C: double the refresh rate the moment the die gets hot. Flip: above 95 C the on-die ECC engine regroups codewords from SEC to a 3-bit-correcting BCH using reserved parity columns, and refresh stays at 1x because weak-cell errors get corrected and scrubbed instead.
why: Avoids the 2x hot-refresh penalty in energy and bandwidth (fact 3) for ~3% capacity reserved.

title: Power-transformer ester oil: single-phase immersion keeps DIMMs cold, PFAS-free
idea: Grid transformers moved to biodegradable natural-ester oils for safe, fire-resistant cooling. Immerse memory modules, heat spreaders removed, in a forced-flow single-phase synthetic-hydrocarbon or natural-ester bath, replacing the fluorocarbon two-phase fluids now being phased out, and hold every DRAM die at a uniform ~40 C.
why: Uniform low temperature removes hot-spot-driven worst-case refresh and the 2x refresh mode above 85 C (fact 3), with no PFAS fluid.

title: Single-electron grains: revive room-temperature polysilicon percolation memory
idea: Inverts 'a bit needs ~30,000 electrons behind a switch': use an ultrathin (~3 nm) polysilicon strip whose natural grains form a percolation channel, where trapping a few electrons on one grain via Coulomb blockade shifts conduction measurably (Yano-type cell); retention is set by the blockade barrier, not a transistor off-state, and strips can be self-aligned sidewalls without fine litho.
why: ~10^11-10^12 bits/cm2 from simple poly deposition and minimal masks, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: large variability needing heavy ECC and mapping, ms-s retention with refresh, temperature sensitivity.

title: Junction-free Ga2O3 back-end access transistor at 4.8 eV bandgap
idea: Intrinsic generation scales as n_i ~ exp(-Eg/2kT), so go past IGZO (~3.2 eV) to ALD amorphous or nanocrystalline Ga2O3 (~4.8 eV). Build n-channel thin-film access transistors below 400 C above the periphery, with no p-n junction at the storage node, and suppress oxygen-vacancy traps with an N2O plasma plus an Al2O3 cap. The only leak paths left are gate-dielectric tunneling and deep-trap emission, and film thickness controls both.
why: Adding 1.6 eV of gap lowers n_i by exp(-1.6/0.052), about 1e-13, so retention becomes capacitor-limited (>1000 s) and refresh nearly vanishes (fact 3). BEOL stacking needs no EUV front-end steps and supports 3D tiers (facts 2, 4).

title: Kodak spatial-ALD with inkjet inhibitors prints maskless low-leakage channels
idea: Kodak's selective-area spatial ALD for printed electronics was shelved along with its display ambitions. Inkjet a polymer inhibitor pattern onto a moving web, then grow ZnO/IGZO and Al2O3 by ALD only where the inhibitor is absent. Access TFTs are built additively with ALD-grade interfaces instead of solution-processed oxide.
why: ALD interfaces give leakage close to vacuum-deposited oxide (<=1e-18 A) while staying printable and maskless, with no photoresist or litho capex. Builds on existing Rochester-area U.S. know-how.

title: Phononic wordlines address rows by acoustic resonance frequency
idea: Effect: piezotronic strain from resonant surface acoustic waves. Each row's access junction sits on a phononic resonator tuned to a unique GHz frequency (512 rows over 1-5 GHz at Q~1000); refresh broadcasts a frequency sequence from one interdigitated transducer and only the resonating row gets enough strain to open, replacing decoded wordline drivers.
why: Periphery and refresh energy (facts 7, 3, 10): row decoders and 3 V wordline drivers leave the refresh path; claims ~10x lower refresh selection energy.

title: Dairy cold-chain milk-run delivers LN2 to cryogenic memory pods
idea: Put capacity-memory sleds in sealed 77 K dewar pods topped up by scheduled liquid-nitrogen deliveries, like a dairy milk-run. Industrial LN2 is a by-product of oxygen plants, so no on-site compressor is needed.
why: Zero refresh power: at 77 K, access-transistor leakage falls by >10 orders of magnitude and retention runs from hours to days, so refresh is disabled. CV^2 energy and wire resistance also drop.

title: Glassblower's indium-free amorphous Ga2O3 ultra-wide-gap access channel
idea: A glassblower knows amorphous networks forgive disorder. Instead of indium-based IGZO, deposit ALD amorphous Ga2O3 or AlGaOx at <400 C as a back-end access channel; its ~4.8 eV gap pushes off-current toward 1e-22 A per cell and it avoids indium, a byproduct metal concentrated in China.
why: Retention of hours removes refresh and lets capacitors shrink, and frees oxide-semiconductor DRAM from indium supply risk (scarce-resource axis).

title: Pyroelectric wordline layer auto-cancels hot-die leakage rise
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. A poled AlScN film in the access gate stack generates bound charge equivalent to a more negative gate bias as temperature rises (~-2 to -4 mV/K), offsetting the access transistor's Vt drop that doubles leakage every ~10 C.
why: Refresh bandwidth (fact 3): flattens retention vs temperature so >85 C operation needs no 2x refresh (10-20% bandwidth); passive, zero power. Risk: pyro charge screening over long times.

title: Turtle-shell back plate that retracts the channel during retention
idea: Random stimulus 'turtle shell': pull in when idle, come out to act. A thin-body access channel sits on a buried per-mat back plate; idle mats drive the plate to -1.5 V, raising Vt ~250 mV (about 3.5 decades of subthreshold current), and an activate command returns the plate to 0 V within ~5 ns through a local driver.
why: Gives retention-time high Vt without paying the on-current penalty of a permanently high-Vt device; subthreshold tail down ~1000x, letting refresh run 10x+ slower (fact 3) and shrinking negative-wordline pumps.

title: JEDEC retention-negotiated refresh replaces fixed 32/64 ms
idea: Worse: standardize the worst-case refresh interval for every die ever made. Flip: a JEDEC spec in which each device advertises its measured, temperature-indexed refresh need and the controller negotiates the interval, with a mandatory on-die guard canary.
why: Industry-wide refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) down ~2x; rewards better access devices commercially.

title: Nanotube-source vertical transistor leakage fixed with capped-source access
idea: Carbon-nanotube-source vertical organic transistors (the CN-VFET line of startups) died on high off-current that flowed straight through the porous source. Electrodeposit a 5 nm insulating cap selectively on top of the printed nanotube mesh, so carriers inject only at the mesh edges under gate control. The result is a vertical, printable access device whose channel length is a film thickness (~100 nm).
why: A short-channel, printable vertical access device with ~1e9 on/off, fast enough for ~100 ns foil memory. It fits compact near-4F2 footprints without lithography.

title: Eliminate the solid channel: vacuum nanogap field-emission access transistor
idea: Isolate each storage node with a 10-20 nm vacuum gap between a sharpened emitter tip and collector, gated by a surrounding electrode; electrons cross only by field emission when the gate thins the barrier. With no semiconductor there is no thermal generation, GIDL or subthreshold conduction.
why: Off current ~1e-21 A lets the capacitor dielectric set retention (minutes+); temperature-immune, ideal for hot AI packages where Si leakage doubles every ~10 C.

title: Metadata replaces refresh: zero-row skip in the memory controller
idea: 10-person constraint: controller logic only. Keep a 1-bit-per-row all-zero bitmap, set by zeroing writes, OS page frees or detected zero rows. Rows marked zero leave the targeted-refresh schedule, and reads to them return zeros from the controller without activating the DRAM.
why: Fact 3: sparse tensors, padding and freshly zeroed pages often leave 10-30% of rows all-zero, and those rows stop costing refresh and activation energy.

title: GE's SCR revived as thyristor RAM cells on U.S. thin-SOI
idea: Revive GE's 1957 silicon-controlled rectifier and the thin-silicon thyristor RAM abandoned around 2012: a gate-coupled pnpn thyristor in thin silicon latches on at a picoamp holding current to store a 1 and stays blocked for a 0, switched by a gate-coupled pulse. Build it on an existing U.S. FD-SOI line.
why: The bistable latch removes refresh (fact 3) and needs no capacitor (fact 1), at near-1T density on a U.S. fab with no EUV; the trade is ~pA-per-bit holding power instead of refresh power.

title: Organic TFT bias-stress killer neutralized by DRAM's tiny duty cycle
idea: Plastic Logic and Polymer Vision died partly because organic TFT thresholds drifted under continuous bias stress. A memory access transistor is on for only nanoseconds per refresh period (duty ~1e-7), and the retention bias can be chosen to anneal any drift back out. Print a wide-gap (~3 eV) small-molecule semiconductor whose tiny intrinsic carrier density gives sub-fA off-current.
why: A printable, solution-coated access device with very low leakage, giving refresh intervals of seconds on foil. It is built from abundant carbon chemistry instead of tungsten-heavy, EUV-patterned stacks.

title: California 'One Watt' standby rule, applied to DRAM self-refresh power
idea: Standby-power regulation (the One Watt Initiative, California Title 20) pushed the appliance industry to redesign idle circuits within a few years. Propose an Energy-Star-style data-center label capping self-refresh/idle power per GB (e.g. <=0.5 mW/GB at 45 C), making low-leakage access devices and adaptive refresh a procurement criterion.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power at 32-64 Gb (fact 3); a standard turns that into a purchasing metric and funds the access-device R&D the market underprices.

title: Resonant LC drivers sweep refresh wordlines adiabatically
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration / resonance: refresh is perfectly periodic and predictable, so drive it with a resonance. Package-level inductors form an LC tank with a bank's refresh wordline and bitline load, so lines rise and fall as sine half-cycles and their energy is recovered rather than dissipated through the ~3 V VPP pump.
why: Attacks the CV^2 floor (Fact 10) and refresh energy (Fact 3): claim 40-60% lower refresh energy without changing the cell.

title: Pendulum maker's LC-resonant wordlines recycle their own swing
idea: A pendulum keeps swinging because energy trades between height and speed. Each bank's wordline drivers share an interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the selected wordline's capacitance; the wordline rises and falls on a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank instead of being dumped to ground, with the pump only topping up losses.
why: A ~3 V wordline fed by ~30%-efficient pumps is a large share of activate energy (fact 10); 85-90% recovery with no pump loss cuts wordline energy ~10x per access.

title: Resonant LC wordline drive recovers refresh energy adiabatically
idea: IFR: refresh energy flows back into the supply. Drive refresh wordlines and the VPP rail from an on-die or interposer inductor that forms an LC tank with the wordline capacitance, ramping over ~5-10 ns so the swing is quasi-adiabatic, then returning the charge to the tank instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Fact 10: the ~3 V wordline CV^2 and charge-pump losses dominate activation energy; recovering 50-70% of it cuts refresh energy ~25-40% and shrinks charge-pump area.

title: CCD memory's junctionless charge wells as refresh-light storage
idea: CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on random access, but their charge sat in potential wells under gates, with no source/drain junction. Store each bit in a buried-channel well under a gate and clock it through a short 4-8 cell chain to a shared sense node. The storage node then has no p-n junction and no GIDL edge, and its only leakage is thermal generation in a fully depleted buried channel.
why: Removes junction and GIDL leakage, the dominant retention tail, for a claimed 10-100x retention gain. It also deletes 7 of every 8 access transistors (density), at the cost of a few ns of shift latency.

title: CD-player C2 flags: sense amps that mark uncertain bits as erasures
idea: CD players mark scratched symbols as erasures so the decoder can fix twice as many. Give the bitline sense amplifier a third 'uncertain' output (a window comparator about +/-20 mV around the reference) so weakly decayed cells reach the decoder as erasures rather than silent errors, doubling correctable bits per parity bit.
why: Fact 3: at fixed parity, refresh can stretch further, or the same 1% cell BER needs about half the parity; costs a few transistors per sense amp.

title: Solexel's porous-silicon lift-off foils as crucible-free low-leakage substrates
idea: Solexel's kerfless epitaxial silicon foils died against cheap Chinese wafers. Grow 20-40 um of epitaxial silicon on a porous-silicon release layer, lift it off, and handle the foils roll-to-roll on carrier tape, reusing each template ~50x. Epi silicon carries little oxygen and metal, so access-transistor junction leakage is lower than on Cz.
why: Fewer Cz ingots mean less demand for Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucibles, and epi material tightens the retention tail. Gives a U.S.-manufacturable foil supply.

title: Argon cluster-ion beam trims access-gate CD map die by die
idea: Ar: measure wordline-recess and fin CDs across each DUV-patterned wafer by scatterometry, then scan an argon gas-cluster ion beam whose local dwell time removes exactly the excess material, flattening the CD map before gate formation (location-specific processing).
why: Across-wafer CD variation widens Vt and the leakage tail (fact 3); flattening it lets DUV arrays approach EUV-grade uniformity, extending refresh ~1.5-2x.

title: Magnify refresh duration, minify energy: adiabatic resonant refresh
idea: Refresh whole banks slowly with microsecond ramps driven by an on-package LC resonator that swings wordlines and bitline precharge sinusoidally and recovers charge each cycle, so dissipation scales as (RC/T)*CV^2 instead of CV^2. Refresh has no latency requirement, so stretching it costs nothing.
why: Refresh energy ~46 fJ/bit -> ~5-10 fJ/bit (5-10x lower).

title: Resonant wordline tank recycles refresh wordline energy
idea: Reverse the energy flow of refresh: because refresh activates rows in a fixed, known sequence, drive the boosted wordlines from an on-die LC tank (thin-film inductor in top metal) that swings each wordline up and returns its charge to the tank on the way down, instead of dumping pumped VPP charge to ground every row.
why: Refresh energy (facts 3, 10): wordline and charge-pump losses at VPP~3 V are a large share of refresh energy; recovering ~50-70% of them cuts refresh energy ~20-30% and shrinks VPP pump area (fact 7).

title: 1 Mb-era fat cell revived at 65 nm, stacked by bonding
idea: Revive 1980s cells with 30+ fF capacitors and long-channel access transistors on existing U.S. 65-90 nm fabs to get second-scale retention, then recover density by hybrid-bonding 8-16 thinned dies into one stack, using a direct-bond process invented in North Carolina.
why: Trades area for retention, so refresh is ~0 (fact 3); avoids EUV entirely (fact 4), and running on depreciated U.S. fabs cuts capital intensity.

title: U.S. 125 C 'hot DRAM' line on mature 40 nm tooling
idea: Worse: leave automotive and defense 125 C memory to a few legacy offshore lines. Flip: stand up a U.S. line on used 40 nm DUV tools making large-Cs (~25 fF) trench cells with thick-oxide, long-channel access devices whose physics already meets 125 C for 10 years, funded by automotive and DoD offtake.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity (fact 4): no EUV, about 1/10 the fab cost, and it frees leading-edge wafers for HBM.

title: Slow-tier thick-oxide cell trades 30 ns for ten-second retention
idea: Time trade inside the access device: a capacity-tier DRAM built with 5-6 nm SiO2, long-channel, high-Vt access transistors at relaxed pitch accepts tRCD ~30-40 ns in exchange for ~10 s retention, with wide parallel interfaces hiding latency for bulk AI weights.
why: Refresh (fact 3) nearly eliminated, and capital (fact 4): the tier can run on depreciated 28-40 nm DUV fabs in the U.S. using only Si, SiO2, TiN, Al and Cu.

title: Semprius transfer printing puts crystalline access transistors on printed capacitors
idea: Semprius's micro-transfer printing died with concentrated PV, not because the stamps failed. Release arrays of single-crystal SOI access transistors (long channel, thick oxide, low leakage) from a donor wafer and stamp them onto a capacitor foil made roll-to-roll. The donor's handle wafer is reused for many foils.
why: Crystalline, low-leakage switches without building a DRAM fab, with capacitors made roll-to-roll. Handle reuse lowers demand for Cz silicon and crucibles.

title: Memory on window glass: multi-tier oxide TFT cells on display lines
idea: Inverts 'memory is made on 300 mm silicon wafers': run 1T1C cells on idle Gen-8.5 to Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED glass lines, stacking 10-20 tiers with KrF-class litho at ~0.3 um and oxide-TFT access whose ultralow leakage lets tiny capacitors skip refresh; dice panels into tiles bonded to a small CMOS controller.
why: Display glass costs ~100-1000x less per area than leading-edge silicon; at 20 tiers and 4F2, ~$0.1-0.4/GB, ~25-100x cheaper; trade-off is ~100 ns-1 us access and lower density per volume.

title: Swap hydrogen for deuterium in the final DRAM anneal
idea: Reverse the isotope: in existing mature DRAM lines, replace the forming-gas hydrogen anneal that passivates interface and STI traps with a high-pressure (~20 atm) deuterium anneal in existing high-pressure anneal tools. Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation far better than Si-H, so fewer traps reactivate into the GIDL and variable-retention-time tail.
why: Leakage tail and VRT (fact 3): a 2-3x smaller tail relaxes refresh ~2x from a single process-step swap; D2 supply is not geographically concentrated.

title: Self-healing tail cells via localized Joule anneal of junction traps
idea: Po: the leakiest cell sets the refresh, so the leakiest cell must heal itself. On-die BIST finds the worst-retention cells and drives a controlled forward current through their storage-node junction, self-heating it to ~400 C for microseconds so hydrogen/deuterium from a reservoir liner re-passivates the trap that causes the tail.
why: Fact 3: refresh rate is set by the <0.01% tail; compressing the tail 4-8x allows ~4x longer refresh interval, cutting refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~75%.

title: Trim each leaky cell's Vt via access-gate charge trap
idea: Substitute worst-case refresh with per-cell repair. The access gate stack includes a thin nitride trap layer; after retention test, the ppm of tail cells are programmed by hot-carrier injection at their bitline-side edge (bitline biased as drain). That raises their source-barrier Vt by ~150-200 mV without adding storage-side GIDL, and the trapped charge holds for years, as in SONOS.
why: The <=13 fA tail sets tREF for every cell; trimming it lets the chip refresh at the median cell's rate: 4-10x fewer refreshes and 10-20% of bandwidth recovered.

title: Minify the access device to nothing: self-rectifying ferroelectric diode crossbar
idea: Use Sc-doped AlN or BiFeO3 ferroelectric layers whose polarization flips the Schottky barrier at one electrode, producing a diode whose forward direction encodes the bit; the cell rectifies itself, so a passive crossbar needs no transistor and stacks in many BEOL layers with non-destructive current read.
why: Removes the access transistor and its leakage; 4F^2 per layer times stacking; non-volatile; avoids destructive read (fact 8).

title: State-dependent in-cell charge pump fed by global keep-alive wave
idea: IFR: every bit refreshes itself at once, with no row activation. Each cell gets a gated diode whose gate is the storage node and whose plate ties to a chip-wide sinusoidal keep-alive plane; a stored '1' forms the diode channel so each AC cycle pumps a few hundred electrons back in, while a '0' forms no channel and nothing is pumped.
why: Fact 3: refresh commands, sense-amp toggling and refresh bandwidth loss vanish; restore costs only a small AC displacement current, an estimated 10-30x less energy than row-by-row refresh.

title: Basket-weave buried wordlines dive and rise to starve passing-gate leakage
idea: Route each buried wordline over-and-under like basket weave: it runs deep beside one storage node and shallow beside the next. No storage node then sits beside a full-depth passing gate whose toggling pumps electrons into it.
why: Facts 3 and 9: passing-gate-induced charge loss is a leakage mechanism behind row hammer. Weave geometry could raise the hammer threshold ~5-10x and remove most targeted-refresh overhead.

title: Magnify the gate-drain underlap to defuse GIDL
idea: Stretch a 15-25 nm ungated, lightly doped drain extension along the vertical pillar between wordline and storage node so peak drain field drops from ~1.5 to <0.6 MV/cm, exponentially suppressing band-to-band (GIDL) and trap-assisted tunneling. A thin fringing field plate tied to the bitline restores on-current.
why: GIDL/TAT dominate the retention tail; 10-100x lower tail current lifts minimum retention and stretches the refresh interval 4-8x.

title: Borrow the image sensor's darkness: pinned storage diode with transfer gate
idea: Limit: the storage node may never touch an oxide interface. Store the bit as electrons in a buried n-well under a p+ pinning layer, as in a 4T CMOS image-sensor pixel, and write and read it through a transfer gate to a floating-diffusion sense node with a gain transistor. Pinning eliminates interface-state generation, which is how image sensors reach dark currents of ~1e-18 A per pixel.
why: Fact 3: dark currents 1000x below the DRAM tail push retention to minutes or hours, and gain readout reduces the charge needed (fact 1). Costs: gain-cell-class area and full-transfer speed.

title: Child's whisper: +/-100 mV storage with auto-zeroed sense amps
idea: A child asks why memory shouts when a whisper carries. Store bits as +/-100 mV around the mid level instead of 0/1.1 V with bitlines parked at mid; chopper/auto-zero sense amplifiers cancel their own offsets to <3 mV each cycle, and a low-Vt access device suffices because the storage node always sits near the bitline potential.
why: Array energy scales as C*V^2: cutting the swing from 1.1 V to 0.2 V lowers cell and bitline energy ~10-30x per access, and the tiny hold Vds also cuts leakage.

title: Minify the charge to a few electrons on Coulomb-blockaded nanodots
idea: Store bits as 5-10 electrons on sub-3 nm Si nanodots whose charging energy (>10 kT) blocks thermally activated escape, sensed non-destructively by a gate-coupled single-electron transistor; writes use direct tunneling through ~2 nm oxide at low voltage, avoiding high-field wear.
why: Non-volatile via quantized charging energy, fJ writes, extreme density; room-temperature uniformity is the risk.

title: Room-temperature Coulomb-blockade box stores bits without a switch
idea: IFR: isolation comes from the electron's own charge. Store each bit as ~20-50 electrons on a sub-2 nm silicon nanocrystal coupled to the bitline by a tunnel junction whose charging energy (>10 kT at 300 K) blocks transport unless a gate pulse aligns the island to a degeneracy point.
why: Fact 3: Coulomb blockade replaces the access transistor as the leakage barrier, with cells potentially under 100 nm^2; dot-size variability and background charge are the risks.

title: Magnify bandgap to 3.3 eV: SiC-junction DRAM holding charge for decades
idea: Build the storage junction and access transistor in 4H-SiC, whose intrinsic carrier density (~1e-9 cm^-3 vs 1e10 for Si) cuts thermal generation current by ~18 orders of magnitude, so a charged node holds >10 years at 85 C with the access device off. The read/write scheme stays DRAM-like and U.S. SiC power-device lines can host it.
why: Data survives power loss and refresh disappears (fact 3); reuses domestic SiC fabs; MOS interface traps and density are the risks.

title: Silicon charge racetrack: CCD loops that refresh by moving
idea: Time shift: rather than holding charge still and refreshing it, data circulates as charge packets in short buried-channel CCD loops (e.g., 16 bits per vertical pillar) clocked at ~1-2 GHz with a regenerative re-inject stage per loop, so every bit is restored each ~10 ns loop and random access waits <=8 ns on average; silicon replaces magnetic racetrack's Co/Pt.
why: Refresh disappears as a separate operation and density rises (~16 bits per footprint, an alternative route around fact 2); Si/O/TiN only; risks are charge-transfer inefficiency and clock power.

title: Eliminate the doped storage-node junction: high-barrier PtSi Schottky contact
idea: Replace the n+ storage-node junction with a self-aligned PtSi or IrSi contact on n-type silicon (barrier ~0.85-0.95 eV), forming a gate-modulated Schottky-barrier access device; in hold, the barrier blocks thermionic emission and there is no junction depletion region to host trap-assisted generation. Silicidation runs below 500 C.
why: Removes the implanted-junction leakage component and yields BEOL-compatible access devices for stacking (facts 2-3); evaporation and furnace only.

title: JEDEC retention-class mode register lets controllers trust each die
idea: Propose and fund a JEDEC ballot that adds a mode-register field where each die reports its own tested retention class per bank (64, 128, 256 or 512 ms at 85 C) from production test. Add a 'relaxed refresh permitted' bit tied to the vendor's warranty. $1M funds reference characterization data, a compliant FPGA controller and two years of standards work.
why: Vendors already measure retention but throw the result away into a worst-case spec. Exposing it lets every controller run at the die's real interval, a fleet-wide 2-4x cut in refresh overhead (fact 3).

title: Silicon-on-sapphire storage nodes on U.S.-grown sapphire
idea: Revive Autonetics' 1963 silicon-on-sapphire, updated with solid-phase regrowth and laser anneal: build the array on sapphire wafers grown in New Hampshire and Illinois, so storage-node diffusions have no junction to a substrate. The insulating substrate also removes substrate-coupled noise and soft-error charge collection.
why: Removes the storage-node-to-substrate junction leakage component (fact 3) and soft errors with U.S. supply: 2-5x longer retention if the regrown silicon quality holds.

title: Sacrificial hydrogen getter keeps oxide-TFT leakage tail low for life
idea: TRIZ #11 Beforehand cushioning: oxide-semiconductor access devices on glass drift leaky as hydrogen, a shallow donor, diffuses in from passivation and packaging. A buried Ti/Zr getter film patterned around each memory tile absorbs that hydrogen over the product life, cushioning the off-current tail before it can move.
why: Holds sub-1e-19 A leakage stable over ten years so refresh can be set in seconds (Fact 3); one cheap sputter step.

title: Rod-and-cone dual-mode back gate for BEOL double-gate access FETs
idea: Retinas switch between fast cones and sensitive rods; make BEOL access FETs double-gate oxide channels whose bottom gate is a shared per-mat plane at 0 V in active mode (low Vt, high Ion) and driven to about -2 V in retention mode, raising Vt ~0.5 V.
why: Separates speed from leakage: active mode performs like a low-Vt device while idle off-current drops ~1e4x, making self-refresh power (16-33% of idle) nearly zero.

title: Retention-mode back-gate swing on double-gate vertical transistors
idea: Worse: use one fixed Vt that must stay low for speed. Flip: in 4F2 vertical-channel arrays, make the shared isolation plate a back gate driven to about -1.5 V in self-refresh (Vt +300 mV, subthreshold leakage about 100x lower) and to 0 V when the bank is active.
why: Idle power share of refresh (16-33%, fact 3); ~10x retention in standby with no speed penalty.

title: Inline e-beam voltage contrast maps junction leakage before capacitor
idea: Box: standard cell x access transistor probed at storage-contact level x e-beam voltage-contrast imaging of charge decay per contact x inline metrology x Si x fab method. Charging each exposed storage contact and imaging its decay over ms maps the leakage distribution on every wafer, feeding implant/anneal recipes in days rather than months of electrical test.
why: Faster learning on the leakage tail (fact 3) shortens yield ramps for new nodes and new US fabs, reducing capital time (fact 4).

title: AMOLED dual-gate TFT trick: breathing back-gate for hold versus access
idea: Display backplanes add a second gate under the TFT to shift its threshold on demand. Give vertical-channel 4F2 access transistors a shared back-gate plate held at about -1 V during retention (raising Vt ~0.3 V, cutting subthreshold leakage ~1000x) and pulsed positive only for the activated mat during access to boost on-current.
why: Decouples off-state leakage from on-current (facts 3, 10): longer refresh intervals and a lower VPP wordline swing because the back-gate supplies the on-boost.

title: Leakage must be a product, not a sum: stacked double-gate pillar
idea: Limit: no single gate may hold off the full voltage. In a vertical-channel 4F2 pillar, split the gate into two stacked electrodes that are driven together to turn on. When off, the mid-channel node floats to an intermediate potential, so each segment sees about half the Vds, and DIBL and GIDL drop superlinearly (the stack effect) at zero added footprint.
why: Fact 3: the stack effect cuts off-current ~10x in logic. In a vertical cell the second gate costs height, not area, so the refresh interval could rise ~5-10x.

title: Ovonic threshold switch recovery-time as a volatile crosspoint bit
idea: Po: the selector remembers that it just fired. After an ovonic threshold switch turns on, its threshold stays lowered for ms before recovering; write a 1 by firing the cell, then read with a pulse between the lowered and recovered thresholds so only recently fired cells conduct, giving a capacitorless, transistorless 4F^2 crosspoint DRAM where refresh means re-firing.
why: Facts 1, 2 and 4: stackable BEOL crosspoint tiers with no capacitor or access transistor; speculative on retention control and read disturb.

title: Eliminate room temperature: 77 K liquid-nitrogen DRAM tier
idea: Run a DRAM pool immersed in liquid nitrogen, where junction and subthreshold leakage fall >1e6x so refresh disappears, and redesign access transistors with low Vt so the wordline drops from 3 V to ~1 V. Pair with cryo-CMOS controllers; LN2 is cheap and helium-free.
why: Refresh eliminated, wordline energy ~9x lower, relaxed Vt allows smaller devices; avoids the helium chokepoint. Cooling overhead (~10 W per W removed) limits it to large pools.

title: Wood-frog freeze-tolerant memory pools at 77 K
idea: Wood frogs survive freezing with metabolism halted; run disaggregated CXL memory pools immersed in liquid nitrogen where junction and subthreshold leakage collapse, switch refresh off, and use access FETs re-targeted to lower Vt using the ~15-20 mV/dec cryogenic slope.
why: Retention grows from 64 ms to hours, removing refresh energy and bandwidth entirely, and VPP can drop ~30-40%; cooler overhead is amortized at rack scale for AI memory.

title: ETA-10 liquid-nitrogen memory tier using U.S. air separation
idea: Revive ETA Systems' 1987 ETA-10 supercomputer, which ran CMOS boards immersed in liquid nitrogen: put DRAM and HBM modules in LN2 baths made on site by U.S. air-separation units. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by >1e6, so refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms to minutes, and lower Vt allows lower wordline voltage.
why: Nearly eliminates refresh (fact 3), and lower voltages cut CV2 (fact 10); nitrogen comes from air, so the cooling needs no helium and has no Qatar exposure.

title: Titan alien's 77 K memory pool with sub-volt wordlines
idea: An alien from 94 K Titan would run memory where its physics is happiest. Pooled DRAM is immersed in liquid nitrogen and the array redesigned for 77 K: subthreshold slope steepens to ~20 mV/dec, so the access threshold drops and the wordline swings 0.8 V instead of a pumped 3 V, VARY falls to ~0.5 V, and leakage-driven refresh disappears.
why: Wordline and array CV^2 plus pump losses fall ~10-20x per access and refresh energy goes to ~0; the cryocooler cost (~5-10 W per W removed) only pays off for large shared pools, so the device-level gain must be big.

title: 77 K co-designed DRAM pool with refresh switched off
idea: Scale jump from device to rack plus a time jump in retention: a CXL memory rack immersed in liquid nitrogen with DRAM redesigned for 77 K, with access-transistor Vt lowered ~0.3 V (subthreshold slope ~20 mV/dec at 77 K), VARY dropped to ~0.6 V and wordline to ~1.8 V, so leakage collapses by >10 decades and refresh is replaced by an hourly scrub.
why: Eliminates refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and breaks the voltage floor (fact 10): ~3-5x lower CV^2 array energy, with cryocooler overhead amortized across a rack-scale shared pool.

title: Liquid-nitrogen immersion DRAM pods eliminate refresh and cut wire energy
idea: N: run pooled CXL memory sleds immersed in 77 K liquid nitrogen made on site from air (no helium); subthreshold and junction leakage fall >10^6 so refresh can be disabled, Vt variation tightens, and copper resistance drops ~5x, enabling lower-swing I/O.
why: Kills refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and lowers data-movement energy (fact 5); cryocooling costs ~10 W per W at 77 K, so the net win targets capacity pools where DRAM idle power dominates.

title: Magnify the threshold during storage with a pulsed back-plate
idea: Give vertical-channel access transistors a buried back-gate plate per subarray held at -1.5 V during retention (raising Vt ~0.4 V by body effect) and pulsed to 0 V only in the subarray being activated. Leakage falls ~10^4x in storage while access on-current is untouched.
why: Breaks the leakage-vs-speed trade-off behind refresh (fact 3); refresh interval 10-50x longer.

title: Leakage-balanced bitline standby voltage cancels junction loss
idea: Box: standard cell x standard access x retuned SA precharge generator x in-array x Si x zero masks. In self-refresh the bitlines park slightly above VDD/2 so subthreshold current flows into 1-nodes and offsets their junction/GIDL loss, while 0-nodes absorb the small extra leak from their larger margin; the park voltage is trimmed per die at test.
why: Balancing the two failure tails extends worst-case retention ~1.5-2x (fact 3) with only a trimmable regulator.

title: Pressure-cooker deuterium anneal replaces fluorine interface passivation of access gates
idea: Pressure cookers cook through at lower temperature by raising pressure. Instead of fluorine implants or F-containing gate stacks, run a 20-25 atm pure-D2 anneal at ~350 C after capacitor and BEOL so deuterium penetrates deep buried-wordline and vertical-channel interfaces that forming gas cannot reach; Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation better than Si-H.
why: Lower, more stable interface-trap density narrows the GIDL/trap-assisted tail (fact 3) by ~1.5-3x with zero fluorinated chemistry.

title: Pulsed-hold thyristor array refreshed blindly without sense amplifiers
idea: Po: refresh without reading. Use vertical gated thyristor latches (no capacitor) but power their anode lines only in short pulses; between pulses an ON cell's base charge decays slowly, and each pulse re-latches every ON cell in the array at once while OFF cells stay off.
why: Fact 3: refresh needs no activate, sense or restore, so it uses no bitline charge or bandwidth, and duty cycling cuts thyristor standby power 10-100x.

title: Resistive-load 4T SRAM revived with printed oxide TFT loads
idea: The 4T SRAM with polysilicon load resistors died because its TOhm loads would not scale and drew standby current. Oxide semiconductors lack a good p-type, so they cannot make CMOS SRAM, but they make superb loads. Print a cross-coupled pair of oxide TFTs whose loads are oxide TFTs in deep subthreshold, sized so the load current (~1e-15 A) exceeds pull-down leakage (~1e-18 A).
why: A static, refresh-free, n-type-only printed cell with ~fW standby per bit, which gets around oxide electronics' missing p-type.

title: Neutral-beam etch of wordline recess removes plasma-induced traps
idea: Box: standard cap x recessed access x SA x in-array x Si x neutral-beam (charge-free, VUV-free) etch replacing RIE for the recess trench, zero masks. Neutral beams avoid the charging and VUV photon damage that seed interface traps on the trench walls forming the channel and storage-junction edge.
why: Fewer interface traps shrink the subthreshold/TAT tail and Vt spread (fact 3), targeting ~2x retention on the same mask set.

title: Plumbing unions for 3D stacks: reworkable low-temperature microbump joints
idea: Adapted from plumbing unions that let one pipe section come out without cutting the rest: bond HBM-style stacks with low-melting In or Sn-Bi microbumps at defined 'union' levels, so a die whose retention fails burn-in or ages in the field can be removed near 150 C and replaced without scrapping the stack.
why: HBM yield is down 20-30% (fact 6), often from one weak die; reworkable unions recover the other dies and let leaky dies (fact 3) be swapped instead of guard-banding refresh for the whole stack.

title: Bottle-deposit systems: refundable deposit funds module retention re-profiling
idea: Adapted from container-deposit schemes: add a refundable deposit (~$2-5) to each memory module, redeemable at certified refurbishers that re-profile retention, remap weak rows and re-grade modules into refresh classes; unredeemed deposits fund the re-test equipment.
why: Most retired DRAM is shredded before anyone checks whether its access devices still retain data (fact 3); a deposit captures modules for re-grading and adds usable supply without new fabs.

title: Wordline-swing ceiling of 1 V: band-to-band tunnel FET access device
idea: Limit: the access device may swing only 1 V yet must still cut off by 10 decades. Use a vertical p-i-n tunnel FET (SiGe source pocket, Si channel, n+ storage-side drain). It turns on by band-to-band tunneling at sub-60 mV/dec and has no thermionic subthreshold tail, so off-current is set by the reverse-biased p-i-n diode (aA range). Asymmetric doping blocks ambipolar leakage from the storage side.
why: Facts 3 and 10: lets VPP drop from 3 V toward ~1.5 V (~4x less wordline CV2) and removes the thermionic tail that forces refresh. A low on-current (~1 uA) still charges 5 fF in under 10 ns.

title: Barrier-free molybdenum buried wordline recessed deeper, tungsten-free
idea: Box: standard cap x buried-channel access with barrier-less Mo wordline x SA x in-array x Si x CVD/ALD Mo using the existing recess pattern (zero added masks). Mo's low narrow-line resistivity without a TiN liner lets the conductor sit further below the storage junction at equal wordline resistance, shrinking gate-storage overlap.
why: Reduced overlap lowers GIDL ~3-5x (fact 3) and removes tungsten (China ~80%) from the densest layer.

title: Z-RAM revival: SiGe hole well keeps floating-body charge
idea: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM died because holes stored in the floating body recombined at the source/drain junctions, and GIDL ate the sense margin as bodies shrank. Grow a 5 nm strained Si0.7Ge0.3 quantum well inside the fully depleted body under a Si cap. Holes then sit in a valence-band pocket ~0.25 eV deep, away from the high-field junction corners where they used to recombine.
why: Capacitorless 1T cell (no capacitor charge wall, 4F2-capable). Band-offset confinement is claimed to raise floating-body retention 10-100x, so refresh energy falls in proportion and the capacitor module is deleted.

title: Floating segment node: cells leak into neighbors, not the bitline
idea: Rearrange the isolation hierarchy: group 4-8 cells on a short local node that connects to the bitline through one segment transistor. In hold the segment device is off, so the local node floats and settles between the cells' stored voltages; each access transistor sees a small Vds, and any path to the bitline must cross two off devices in series (stack effect).
why: Subthreshold leakage (fact 3) falls ~5-10x via stack effect and reduced Vds/DIBL, stretching refresh ~3-5x; the segment switch also cuts bitline load per access.

title: Cubic-zirconia skull melting: crucible-free silicon with fewer oxygen-related leakage traps
idea: Synthetic-gem makers melt zirconia inside a crust of its own frozen material in a water-cooled copper 'cold crucible'. Grow DRAM-grade silicon by cold-crucible induction Czochralski, eliminating the Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucible and its oxygen supply, and engineer gettering with nitrogen/carbon co-doping instead of oxygen precipitates.
why: Lower interstitial oxygen means fewer oxygen-related defects and thermal donors near junctions (narrower tail, fact 3) and removes a >80% single-source chokepoint; crystal growth stays fluorine-free.

title: Microwave oven annealing: low-temperature regrowth of storage junction damage
idea: Microwave ovens heat what absorbs, not the whole kitchen. Activate storage-node dopants and regrow amorphized silicon by 2.45/5.8 GHz microwave annealing at 400-500 C, where dipole-assisted solid-phase epitaxy avoids the end-of-range loops and diffusion of spike anneals, replacing the fluorine co-implants used to suppress those defects.
why: Fewer end-of-range dislocation loops near the junction shrinks the generation-leakage tail (fact 3); the low temperature also suits monolithically stacked tiers (fact 2).

title: Hot-isostatic-press deuterium loads buried channels of deep 3D stacks
idea: Borrow HIP, which closes casting voids: 20-100 atm D2 at ~350 C forces deuterium through 26+ tiers to passivate dangling bonds in buried lateral channels that ordinary forming gas never reaches. Deuterium's mass also resists hot-carrier depassivation.
why: Fact 2/3: equalizes the leakage tail between top and bottom tiers of 3D DRAM, plausibly 2-5x in deep tiers.

title: Eliminate the wordline wire: light-gated wide-bandgap photoconductive access switch
idea: Replace the electrical wordline with a SiN waveguide row that delivers a nanosecond UV or blue pulse to ZnO or GaN photoconductive switches at each cell; in the dark the wide-gap switch has essentially no carriers and no leakage. The waveguide is passive, so wordline RC delay and 3 V pumps disappear.
why: Removes wordline drivers and high-voltage pumps (facts 7, 10) plus the leakage tail; SiN waveguides and sputtered ZnO are university processes; optical energy per access is the risk.

title: Magnify endurance with antiferroelectric ZrO2 given a built-in bias
idea: Antiferroelectric ZrO2 survives 1e12+ cycles but has no remanence; asymmetric electrodes (TiN vs RuO2 work-function offset) plus a fixed-charge dipole interlayer shift the double loop so one AFE loop straddles zero field, creating two stable remanent states.
why: Non-volatile cells with endurance 100-1000x beyond HZO FeRAM; refresh-free.

title: Hermetic NEMS relay access switch: an air gap is the perfect off-state
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution, inverted: replace the field-effect switch with an electrostatically actuated nano-cantilever relay built on glass and sealed in a vacuum/inert micro-cavity. Open, the gap gives zero channel leakage so retention is set only by capacitor dielectric leakage (minutes to hours); closed, a metal contact gives near-ideal write/read with abrupt switching at low actuation voltage.
why: Eliminates the access-transistor leakage tail entirely (Fact 3) and the 3 V wordline (Fact 10) via abrupt actuation; key risks are contact endurance at 1e12-1e15 cycles and ns-scale switching.

title: Goto-pair tunnel-diode static cell with picoamp valley hold
idea: Po: two leaks fight and the bit is whoever wins. Series-connect two nanoscale Esaki tunnel diodes as a Goto pair between rails so their negative-differential-resistance curves cross at two stable points; the midpoint node holds the bit statically behind one access transistor, with standby set by valley current scaled to pA.
why: Facts 1 and 3: capacitorless static storage with no refresh; ~8F^2 if diodes stack vertically; risk is valley current and peak-current uniformity.

title: LCD panel laser repair: spot-anneal the retention-tail cells
idea: Adapted from the laser repair stations that fix defective TFT pixels in LCD fabs: after retention test, or at a refurbisher, a nanosecond laser heats ~1 um spots containing weak cells through a thinned backside in forming gas, annealing the traps that cause their leakage.
why: Repairs the leakage tail (fact 3) of finished dies without spending spare rows; LCD fabs run such tools at high throughput, and repair can be repeated at end of first life before resale.

title: Magnify ECC to a full 8 KB row LDPC merged with refresh
idea: Store ~3% row-length LDPC parity inside each row and stretch refresh to 1-2 s; every refresh activation decodes on-die and writes back corrected bits, so refresh doubles as scrubbing and retention-tail errors never accumulate.
why: Refresh interval 16-32x longer: refresh bandwidth and energy down >90% for ~3% area.

title: Magnify the retention tail into a product: long-retention premium bin
idea: Measure each die's retention distribution at wafer sort and sell the top-quartile dies as 'LR' parts with a guaranteed 256 ms-1 s refresh spec at a premium to hyperscalers; controllers read the bin and lengthen tREFI accordingly.
why: Monetizes existing variation: 4-16x less refresh on LR parts, more effective bandwidth and lower power without new fabs.

title: Eliminate the incumbents' data monopoly: open 1-um access-device PDK across universities
idea: Publish an open process kit for 100 mm wafer access devices (Si, SiC, Ga2O3 variants) runnable in ten U.S. university nanofabs, each running monthly shuttles with standardized retention-tail test structures; pooled data on millions of cells reveal which elimination (junction, oxide, body) shrinks the tail.
why: Breaks the barrier that only three firms see leakage-tail statistics at scale; accelerates U.S. access-device innovation for ~$10M/yr instead of a $15B fab.

title: Junctionless storage node removes the leakage-tail junction
idea: Reverse the doping layout: make the access device a uniformly n-doped ultrathin (<=5 nm) junctionless channel that turns off by full depletion under a wraparound gate, so there is no n+/p metallurgical junction at the storage node. Trap-assisted junction leakage and junction-field GIDL, the main sources of the retention tail and variable retention time, lose their high-field region.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): removing the storage-node junction field could cut tail leakage ~10x and shrink VRT, relaxing refresh ~4-8x.
